subtype: Approach: copies a successful company's plan without its context [Pitfall]
passage: When my co-founder Tanuja and I started our tiny design studio, there were three of us, including our first hire. I'm Rukmini. We needed one more designer, and I did what I thought serious companies did. I found a big tech firm's hiring guide online and copied it: an online aptitude test, a take-home assignment, two technical rounds, a culture interview and a panel with all three of us. Only we had no budget for test software, so I built the aptitude test myself, which took a week. Candidates dropped out after the take-home. The panel round meant stopping client work for a whole day, three times. After six weeks we still hadn't hired anyone. Tanuja finally said, "We're three people. We need one good conversation and a paid trial day."

qa.q: How many weeks had passed without a hire?
qa.a: After six weeks they still hadn't hired anyone.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel copying the big firm's hiring guide?
qa.a: Rukmini felt it made them look serious, and was probably anxious to do things properly.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: A process built for a large firm didn't fit three people with no budget; a short conversation and a trial day, as Tanuja suggested, would fit.

qa.q: How did the candidates experience the process?
qa.a: Candidates found it long for such a small studio, and many dropped out after the take-home assignment.

grounding: A small start-up copies a large firm's hiring process despite having three people and no budget, and wastes weeks.

passage:
Incubator mentor's note: Siddharth and Mohit, month four

Their start-up has three employees and very little money. They want to hire one sales person. Siddharth showed me their process: five rounds, a psychometric test, a case study, a presentation to "the leadership team", and reference checks. He told me it was copied from a large consulting firm he admired. In practice, the leadership team is Siddharth and Mohit. They have spent three weeks on it; the two strongest candidates accepted other offers while waiting. Mohit looked tired and said he had written the case study twice. I asked them what their company actually needs from this hire, and suggested they design a process that fits three people, not three thousand.

qa.q: How many rounds did their hiring process have?
What does Mohit's tiredness suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He seems worn out and frustrated, having written the case study twice for a process that isn't working.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth and Mohit do to hire faster?
qa.a: Hold one real conversation about the sales role and a short paid trial, focusing on what their company needs.

qa.q: How might the two strong candidates have seen the process?
qa.a: They likely felt it was slow and oversized for a tiny start-up, so they accepted other offers.

grounding: A mentor notes a three-person start-up copying a large firm's hiring process and losing weeks and good candidates.
